subject: Chemistry
title: E-Ink: Color Without Backlight
description: A micro-lesson that makes E-Ink: Color Without Backlight usable.

hook.text: E-readers display text using tiny charged particles that flip between black and white. No backlight means no eye strain.

buildup.text: Each pixel is a microcapsule containing black and white charged particles suspended in clear fluid.

discovery.text: Apply a positive charge: white particles rise. Negative charge: black rises. The image stays with zero power.

twist.text: Color E-Ink adds a filter layer over the capsules. But it cuts brightness by 75%, making colors muted.

climax.text: New Gallery 3 E-Ink uses colored particles instead of filters. Full-color e-readers are finally becoming vivid.

punchline.text: Charged particles in tiny capsules. A display that uses power only when it changes.

quiz.question: Why do E-Ink displays use almost no power?
options: The image stays visible without power; energy is only needed to change it
The backlight is extremely dim compared to LCD screens
The display turns off between page refreshes

details.summary: E-ink displays use millions of microcapsules containing charged black and white pigment particles suspended in a clear fluid. Applying electric fields pushes either black or white particles to the surface. The display uses no backlight and consumes power only when changing the image.
details.whyItMatters: E-ink transformed reading technology with displays that are readable in direct sunlight like paper and have batteries lasting weeks. Color e-ink is now expanding into signage and wearable devices.
takeaways: Charged pigment particles move in electric fields within microcapsules
E-ink displays require power only when the image changes
Color e-ink adds a filter layer over black and white microcapsules

faq.question: Why are e-ink displays easier to read in sunlight than phone screens?
faq.answer: E-ink is reflective, using ambient light like paper, while phone screens emit their own light that gets washed out by sunlight. In bright conditions, e-ink actually becomes more readable as more light reflects off the pigment particles, just as paper does.

faq.question: Why has color e-ink taken so long to develop compared to black-and-white?
faq.answer: Color e-ink requires either color filter arrays over black-and-white particles, reducing brightness by two-thirds, or multiple colored particle types in each capsule that are harder to control precisely. Both approaches sacrifice some of the crispness and contrast of monochrome e-ink.
